extracted.intended_audience: general literate public / readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century readers interested in moral and social commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted guidance and evaluative principles embedded in Spectator essays and letters on topics such as virtue vs. vice, novelty, news, courtship, and petitions for office. The page blends moral argument, practical advice, and satirical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience selection for advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice intended for the 'Idle' (those who 'propose to themselves no End' and 'run adrift with every Wind') will be wasted on them; they 'would scarce take the Pains to read it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'fatigue' the idle with long exhortations. Recognize audience dispositions: long moral harangues are unlikely to reach people described as 'Fools at large' (Dr. Tillotson). Prefer brevity or different strategies for that audience; the essay cites Plato's maxim that 'Labour is preferable to Idleness, as Brightness to Rust' as a succinct corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare labour required by vice and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The same, if not greater, labour is required in the service of Vice and Folly as of Virtue and Wisdom: 'Whether he walks in the Paths of Virtue or Vice, he is sure to meet with many Difficulties to prove his Patience, and excite his Industry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When persuading people to be virtuous, emphasize that vice is not an easier path — show that vice entails comparable or greater effort and suffering, so choosing virtue entails no loss of labour but promises better reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of avarice (how to judge a miser's life)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Miser is more industrious than the Saint: 'The Pains of getting, the Fears of losing, and the Inability of enjoying his Wealth, have been the Mark of Satyr in all Ages.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate avarice by tallying its psychological and practical costs (repentance over bargains, fear of loss, inability to enjoy). The essay draws parallels to St. Paul's catalogue of sufferings to show these are real burdens that could be redirected toward Christian virtues or heavenly 'treasures.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of ambition (how to judge ambition's burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambition's toils may outweigh its fruits: less trouble is needed to deserve lasting glory than to obtain temporary power and reputation; Cardinal Woolsey's regret ('Had I served God, with the same Application, wherewith I served my King, he would not have forsaken me in my old Age') is given as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ambition by its long-term costs (loss of spiritual comfort, insecurity when fortunes change). Counsel that devotion to religion or virtue would have yielded more stable consolation than secular ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of sensual pleasure (how to judge a life of pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of pleasure undergo many pains: 'The Infidelities on the one Part between the two Sexes, and the Caprices on the other, the Debasement of Reason, the Pangs of Expectation, the Disappointments in Possession, the Stings of Remorse, the Vanities and Vexations...' render sensual life 'silly and uncomfortable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sensual pursuits, count emotional labour (expectation, disappointment, remorse) and social costs (caprices, infidelities). Use these features to argue that sensual life may be more painful than it appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical decision criterion: choose virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Because active life requires labour whether in vice or virtue, one has an easy choice: use one’s strength to 'purchase Happiness' (virtue) rather than 'Repentance' (vice): 'he hath this easie Choice left him, whether with the Strength he is Master of, he will purchase Happiness or Repentance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a moral maxim, present virtue as the rational choice by showing equivalence of effort and superiority of outcome (happiness vs repentance). This is intended as a practical decision rule for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating suitors / romantic signals (love-casuist Q&A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of terse answers to common courtship signs (all answered 'No'): e.g., 'When Mr. Fondle looks upon me for half an Hour together, and calls me Angel, is he not in Love?' — No. 'May I be certain he will be a kind Husband, that has promised me half my Portion in Pin-money, and to keep me a Coach and Six?' — No. 'Whether I am old enough to chuse for my self?' — No. etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take surface behaviors or flattering words as proof of sincere or suitable intentions. Material promises, prolonged looks, pitying sighs, gifts (a lock of hair), or the claimant's dramatic threats (drowning) are unreliable indicators. Parental judgment and prudence should carry weight (especially for very young persons). The implied rule: demand substantive proof of character and prudence over affectation or display.

rubrics_metrics.name: News reporting: primacy of timeliness and freshness
rubrics_metrics.description: A correspondent boasts of being 'early in the Antichamber' and 'spare no Pains to know how the World goes. A Piece of News loses its Flavour when it hath been an Hour in the Air. I love... to have it fresh from the Tree; and to convey it to my Friends before it is faded.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat timeliness and freshness as the chief virtues of news: be physically present at gathering points (coffee-houses, antechamber), move quickly between sources, and prioritize beating rival outlets ('forestall the Evening-Post'). The letter even justifies expense (coach-hire) to secure speed. Implicit anti-pattern: stale, secondhand news loses value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of novelty to engage and to drive learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty has a powerful and extensive influence: it 'awakens Desire, enhances Delight, kindles Anger, provokes Envy, inspires Horror' and is the source of Admiration; it also supplies the initial exquisite pleasure that prompts philosophical disquisition and continued inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To engage readers or learners, introduce novelty — new surprises and fresh perspectives stimulate passions and curiosity. But beware the downside: excessive craving for novelty leads to impatience with sustained inquiry, premature confidence ('We see a little, presume a great deal, and so jump to the Conclusion'), and failure to master subjects. Balance novelty-induced engagement with sufficient time for depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty reduces the perceived value of status symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Habit and novelty together 'annihilate all the boasted Distinctions among Mankind' — titles, buildings, furniture, and equipage dazzle everyone but the possessor, who by custom sees them as cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging social distinction or attempting to impress, realize that habituation blunts admiration; novelty (unexpectedness) often matters more than ostentatious possessions. Implicitly, appeals to vanity via status symbols are less effective than offering novel delights or experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for awarding offices, preferments, or recompense
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufferings or claims to reward have merit only when 'they are such as have promoted a good Cause, and fallen upon a Man undeservedly' — sufferings due to rashness or indiscretion do not justify recompense ('they only serve to recommend them to the Children of Violence or Folly').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate petitions for office by (a) whether the claimant's suffering was for a legitimately good cause and undeserved, (b) the sincerity and prudence of the claimant's conduct, and (c) avoid rewarding trivial, self-inflicted, or purely ceremonial acts (satirical examples include roasting an ox, toasting healths, or letting a beard grow). Use merit and desert rather than mere notoriety or theatrical loyalty as criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting responses when solicited for a place
rubrics_metrics.description: Social risk in replies: 'A plain Answer, with a Denial in it, is looked upon as Pride, and a civil Answer as a Promise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to solicitations for preferment, be aware that plain refusals may be interpreted as arrogance while polite or civil responses may be construed as promises. This is a practical communicative rule about how statements will be socially read; manage expectations accordingly.
